judge_reason: Dorman is an automotive aftermarket replacement-parts supplier, while ITT's main business is engineered flow-control and transportation/industrial components rather than the same replacement-parts order. Both can reach automotive aftermarket distributors and channels, but that overlap is less explicit.

Dorman is a branded automotive replacement-parts maker/seller, while DSGR's main business is distributing broad MRO and industrial supplies. Both sell goods, but DSGR is principally a distributor and its listed vehicle repair-shop buyers are not clearly Dorman's retailer, wholesaler, and warehouse-distributor buyers.

Dorman supplies automotive and heavy-duty replacement parts, while CSW’s main business is HVAC/R, plumbing, electrical and industrial products. Both sell manufactured goods through distribution, but their end markets and purchasing buyers are distinct.

Compared Dorman’s automotive/heavy-duty replacement parts business with PSI’s engine and power-system manufacturing business. PSI’s main OEM industrial-equipment buyers do not place the same aftermarket-parts orders or buy in the same role as Dorman’s parts-channel customers.

Compared Dorman’s aftermarket automotive and truck replacement-parts business with Federal Signal’s main business of specialized municipal/industrial vehicles and safety equipment. They both sell manufactured goods, but their products and core purchasing buyers do not overlap.

Compared Dorman's automotive and heavy-duty replacement-parts business with Astec's road-construction and aggregate-processing equipment business. Astec's main buyers procure infrastructure machinery, not automotive aftermarket parts, even though both primarily sell manufactured goods through B2B channels.

Compared Dorman's automotive and heavy-duty replacement-parts business with G-III's branded apparel business. Both sell sourced goods as brand owners, but their products and retail buyers are distinct.

Dorman’s main business is branded automotive and truck replacement parts sold through aftermarket parts channels, while THOR’s main business is manufacturing RVs for RV dealers. Both principally sell manufactured goods, but their products and buying channels differ.

Dorman sells replacement automotive and truck parts through the vehicle-parts aftermarket, while AerSale's main business serves commercial aircraft with used material, aircraft assets, leasing, and MRO. Their buyers and aftermarket roles are distinct, and AerSale's mixed sales, leasing, and service model differs from Dorman's goods sales.

Compared Dorman's automotive and heavy-duty replacement-parts business with Deere's agricultural, construction, forestry and turf equipment business. Deere's main buyers purchase equipment through its dealer network, not the auto-parts-channel replacement orders Dorman serves.

Dorman sells branded replacement automotive parts through aftermarket channels, while Proficient Auto Logistics transports finished new vehicles to dealers. Their buyers and revenue models differ: parts-channel goods sales versus vehicle-shipping services.

Compared Dorman's automotive and heavy-duty replacement parts business with Simpson's construction connectors and fasteners business. Both sell manufactured goods, but their products and the buyers/distribution channels they serve are distinct.

Compared Dorman's automotive and heavy-duty replacement-parts business with Alliance Laundry's commercial and residential laundry-equipment business. They both sell manufactured goods through distribution channels, but auto-parts trade buyers cannot place the same order with Alliance and are not the laundromat, institutional-laundry, or appliance buyers it serves.

Dorman sells automotive and heavy-duty replacement parts to aftermarket parts channels, while Flowserve’s main business is engineered flow-control equipment for industrial operators and EPCs. Both primarily sell manufactured goods and sit at the maker/brand-owner step, but their products and buyers do not overlap.

Dorman sells branded automotive and heavy-duty replacement parts to the vehicle-parts aftermarket, while MSC distributes industrial MRO tools and supplies to manufacturers and maintenance operations. Both sell goods, but they serve different buyers and sit at different chain steps.

Compared Digi's IoT connectivity hardware and device-management offering with Progress's enterprise application and data-infrastructure software. They reach overlapping enterprise IT buyers, but do not offer substitutable products and earn chiefly through different models.

Digi sells IoT connectivity hardware and management tools, while NetApp's main business is enterprise data-storage systems and cloud storage, so a buyer cannot place the same order. Both sell technology infrastructure to enterprise and government IT buyers, primarily as branded products/software and related services.

Compared Digi's IoT connectivity hardware and cloud management with Viavi's network test, monitoring and assurance equipment. They serve overlapping network engineering and enterprise/telecom buyers, but a customer cannot substitute Viavi's main testing products for Digi's routers or embedded connectivity products.

Digi sells IoT connectivity hardware and management tools, while Viasat's main business is satellite broadband and communications services. Enterprise and government network buyers can buy from both, but the products, primary revenue model, and operating position differ.

Digi sells general-purpose IoT connectivity hardware and management software, while Gogo’s main business is providing installed inflight connectivity services to business aircraft. Their buyer groups overlap only broadly through OEM and government categories, not clearly in the same buying role.

Digi sells IoT connectivity hardware and network-management software, while Eastern's main business is engineered industrial hardware, locks and castings. Their OEM exposure is in some of the same industries, but not to the same buying need or buyer role.

Digi sells IoT connectivity and remote-device networking products, whereas NCR Voyix's main business is commerce/POS software and self-service systems, so they are not substitutes. Retailer IT buyers can buy both companies' offerings, and both combine technology product sales with recurring software/services.

Compared Digi's IoT connectivity hardware and network-management offerings with ESCO's aerospace components, utility diagnostic equipment, and RF test products. The products are not substitutable, but utility, OEM, industrial, and technical engineering buyers can overlap; both principally manufacture and sell goods.

Digi designs and sells branded IoT connectivity equipment, while EACO's main business is distributing electronic components and hardware. OEM procurement buyers can buy from both, but EACO is a distributor rather than the equipment maker.

Digi sells IoT connectivity hardware and related management software, while Amdocs mainly provides telecom billing, CRM, and network software/services. Their core buyers and buying roles differ, as do their primary revenue models and chain steps.

Digi's IoT connectivity hardware is not substitutable for SPX's main HVAC and detection/measurement products. However, utilities, industrial operators and public infrastructure buyers can buy both companies' equipment; both primarily manufacture and sell goods.

Digi’s main business is IoT connectivity hardware and cloud management, while Crane mainly makes aerospace components and industrial flow-control equipment. Although both manufacture and sell engineered goods to businesses, their buyers procure for different technical needs and roles.

Compared Digi's IoT networking hardware and cloud management business with Powell's custom electrical power-distribution equipment business. Their products serve different buyer roles—IT/connectivity versus electrical-power engineering—despite some overlap in industrial and utility end markets.

Compared Digi's IoT connectivity hardware and device-management offerings with Autodesk's design, engineering and construction software. They serve different buying roles and orders, and Digi chiefly sells products while Autodesk chiefly earns subscription revenue, though both develop their own offerings.

Digi sells IoT connectivity hardware and network-management software, while AMETEK's main business is industrial instruments, sensors, test equipment and engineered components. Both manufacture and sell goods, but their overlapping industrial/OEM markets do not establish the same buyers in the same buying role.

Compared Par Pacific’s refinery-led production and fuel sales with Chesapeake Utilities’ regulated natural-gas, electric and propane distribution. Commercial and industrial energy buyers can buy from both, but the main products, revenue model and chain role differ.

Compared Par Pacific's refining and fuel sales with Gencor's manufacture of asphalt-mixing equipment. They both sell manufactured goods, but fuel buyers are not buying road-construction plants or related equipment.

Compared Par Pacific's refining and fuel sales business with Avista's regulated electric and natural-gas utility. Commercial and industrial energy buyers can buy from both, but refined fuels are not Avista's main product and the revenue models and chain roles differ.

Compared Par Pacific's refined-fuel production and fuel sales with Astec's road-building and aggregate equipment manufacturing. They sell different products to different buying roles, despite both principally earning revenue by selling manufactured goods.

Par Pacific primarily refines and sells petroleum fuels, while New Jersey Resources primarily distributes regulated natural gas. Their main products, buyer roles, revenue model, and chain position differ.

Compared Par Pacific's refining and fuel sales with Proficient Auto Logistics' finished-vehicle trucking. They serve different buyers with different products and earn revenue at different points in unrelated supply chains.

Par Pacific refines, distributes and sells petroleum fuels, while Construction Partners primarily performs infrastructure construction and paving work. Their products, buyers, revenue sources and primary chain roles do not overlap.

Par Pacific primarily refines and sells petroleum fuels, while RGC Resources is a regulated local natural-gas distribution utility. Their commercial/industrial customer categories do not establish the same buyers buying for the same need.

Par Pacific refines and sells transportation fuels, while BKV mainly produces upstream natural gas and natural gas liquids. Both principally sell energy commodities, but to different buyers and at different points in the value chain.

Compared Par Pacific's refining and fuel sales with PSI's manufacture of engines and power systems. Fuel buyers cannot buy the same order from PSI, and the relevant procurement buyers differ despite some shared industrial end markets.

Par Pacific primarily refines and sells petroleum fuels, while DXP distributes industrial MRO equipment, pumps and related services. Both predominantly sell goods, but their products, buying roles, and main chain positions differ.

Par Pacific refines and sells finished transportation fuels, while Kinetik provides midstream gathering, processing, and pipeline services to upstream producers. Their buyers, revenue mechanisms, and positions in the petroleum value chain differ.

Par Pacific primarily refines and sells transportation fuels, while Quaker Houghton makes industrial process fluids and specialty chemicals. Their buyers purchase for different operational needs and roles, despite both principally manufacturing and selling physical products.

Par Pacific refines and sells transportation fuels, while Trinity’s main business is railcar leasing, manufacturing, and related services. Energy companies may appear in both customer lists, but buy fuel from Par Pacific and rail equipment or leases from Trinity in different roles.

Par Pacific refines and sells transportation fuels, while Core Laboratories provides reservoir-analysis and production-enhancement services. Their principal buyers and positions in the oil-and-gas chain are different.

Accendra distributes home respiratory and durable medical equipment directly to patients, while Solventum mainly manufactures medical-surgical, dental, software, and filtration products. Payers can buy from both, but Solventum is principally a manufacturer whereas Accendra is a home-care supplier.

Accendra supplies durable respiratory and sleep equipment directly to home patients, while Teleflex mainly manufactures single-use devices for hospital use. Their buyers and chain positions differ, although both principally earn from selling medical products.

Accendra distributes home respiratory, sleep, and durable medical equipment, while Chemed's main business provides hospice care (alongside plumbing services). Terminally ill hospice patients are not the same buyers as Accendra's home-equipment patients; shared Medicare/Medicaid payment does not establish customer overlap.

Accendra supplies respiratory, sleep and durable medical equipment directly to home patients, while ICU Medical manufactures hospital infusion systems and IV devices. Their primary buyers and chain roles differ, though both principally earn revenue by selling medical products.

Accendra distributes home respiratory, sleep-therapy, and durable medical equipment to patients, while Brookdale operates senior-living communities providing housing and care services. Their buyers and primary revenue models differ.

Compared Accendra's direct-to-home respiratory, sleep-therapy and durable medical equipment supply business with Labcorp's diagnostic laboratory and contract-research services. Referring clinicians and health systems can use both, but lab testing is a different service delivered at a different chain step and revenue model.

Accendra supplies home respiratory, sleep and durable medical equipment directly to home patients, whereas Merit manufactures procedure devices for hospitals and clinicians. Both primarily sell medical goods, but at different points in the care and supply chain to different buying roles.

Accendra supplies home respiratory, sleep and durable medical equipment to patients, while TruBridge provides EHR, billing and financial-services software to hospitals and clinics. Their buyers and revenue models differ, and TruBridge is not in the home-medical-equipment supply chain.

Accendra supplies home medical equipment and respiratory/sleep therapy directly to patients, while CorVel’s main business is managed care and claims administration. Commercial insurers can buy from both, but for different offerings and at different chain steps.

Accendra supplies and services home respiratory, sleep and durable medical equipment directly to patients, while Masimo mainly manufactures patient-monitoring technologies and sensors. They both sell medical goods, but Masimo is a manufacturer selling primarily to clinical providers rather than a home-equipment supplier.

Compared Accendra’s home-delivered respiratory/DME supplies with RadNet’s outpatient diagnostic-imaging services. The products and economics differ, but referring physicians, health systems and health plans can buy or refer to both in the same care-delivery role.

Compared Accendra's home-delivered respiratory/DME supplies with UniFirst's uniform and facility-services business. The products and buying roles are distinct; UniFirst mainly earns recurring uniform-rental and laundering-service revenue.

Accendra distributes home respiratory, sleep-therapy and durable medical equipment to patients, while Organogenesis manufactures regenerative wound-care and surgical biologics. Their physician and hospital relationships involve different buying roles, and Organogenesis is a manufacturer rather than a home-equipment distributor.

Accendra supplies home respiratory, sleep-therapy, and durable medical equipment to patients, while National Healthcare Properties owns and leases healthcare real estate. Its tenants are healthcare operators and physician practices, not Accendra's equipment buyers or payers.

Accendra supplies home respiratory, sleep, and durable medical equipment directly to patients, while AMS leases radiosurgery systems to hospitals and cancer centers. The equipment, buyer roles, revenue model, and position in the care-delivery chain differ.

Smart Sand sells frac sand, while Solaris's main business rents mobile power-generation fleets; its proppant-handling equipment is a separate, smaller line. Oilfield completion and pressure-pumping buyers can buy from both, but the revenue model and chain step differ.

Smart Sand supplies frac sand and logistics to well-completion buyers, while Weatherford's main business is engineered oilfield equipment and field services. They sell to the same oil-and-gas operator buyers, but not the same order or primarily at the same chain step.

Compared Smart Sand's frac-sand proppant business with Flotek's specialty oilfield-chemistry business. They sell different inputs, but oilfield service companies and energy producers buy from both; both principally manufacture and sell goods.

Smart Sand sells frac-sand proppant and related logistics, while Core Laboratories' main business is reservoir analysis and oilfield technical services. Their oil-and-gas operators and service-company buyers overlap, but the products, revenue model, and chain role do not.

Smart Sand mines and sells frac and industrial sand, while Granite's main business is heavy civil construction. Granite's materials operations serve construction buyers, not Smart Sand's oilfield and industrial-sand buying roles.

Smart Sand mines and sells frac sand to E&P and pressure-pumping customers, while Par Pacific’s main business refines and sells transportation fuels. They both sell manufactured/processed goods, but the products and buying roles do not overlap.

Smart Sand primarily sells frac-sand goods to completion customers, while Kinetik’s main business is fee-based midstream gathering, processing, and transportation. Though both serve E&P companies, the relevant buying roles and offerings differ.

Smart Sand produces frac sand for oilfield completion customers, while Oil-Dri's main business is sorbent-clay products such as cat litter and industrial absorbents. Both sell manufactured mineral goods and mine/process the underlying minerals, but the products and buying roles differ.

Smart Sand produces and sells frac/industrial sand, while Ecovyst's main business is specialty catalysts and sulfuric-acid chemicals and regeneration. Both manufacture and sell industrial materials, but their buyers and products do not overlap in the same purchasing role.

Smart Sand sells frac-sand proppant and delivery solutions, while NGS's main business is renting and servicing natural-gas compression equipment. Both sell to oil and gas producers, but for different operational needs and with different primary revenue models.

Smart Sand mines and sells frac sand/proppant to oilfield buyers, while BBCP's main business is contractor-operated concrete pumping for construction projects. They serve different buyer roles and earn revenue through goods sales versus services.

Smart Sand mines, processes, and sells frac/industrial sand, while Astec’s main business is manufacturing infrastructure and aggregate-processing equipment. They both sell goods they make, but serve different buying roles and needs.

Smart Sand produces and sells frac sand to oilfield operators and pressure pumpers, while LSB's main business is nitrogen fertilizers and industrial/mining chemicals. Both manufacture and sell goods, but their products and buying roles do not overlap.

Smart Sand sells frac and industrial sand, while Quaker Houghton’s main business is industrial process fluids and specialty chemicals. Their core buyers are oilfield operators and pressure pumpers versus metals and manufacturing users, respectively.

Compared Smart Sand's mined and processed frac-sand supply business with DXP's industrial MRO and pump distribution business. They sell different orders to different buying roles, and Smart Sand produces proppant while DXP distributes equipment and supplies.

Greif’s main business is industrial packaging for manufacturers, whereas Reynolds mainly makes household foil, bags and disposable tableware for retailers and consumers. Both manufacture and sell goods, but their products and buying customers differ.

Greif manufactures industrial packaging, while DXP’s main business is distributing MRO equipment and pumps. Their industrial customers may overlap at the company level, but packaging procurement buyers are not the same buying role as DXP’s maintenance and equipment buyers.

Greif manufactures industrial packaging containers and related services, while PPG's main business is paints and coatings. Both manufacture and sell goods, but their products and the relevant purchasing buyers are different.

Greif makes industrial containers and packaging, while Veralto's main businesses are water analytics/treatment and product-identification equipment, not substitute packaging. Manufacturers' packaging and plant-operations buyers can buy Greif containers and Veralto coding/marking systems, and both principally manufacture and sell goods.

Compared Greif's industrial packaging manufacturing with Carlisle's commercial roofing and building-envelope materials business. Their products and primary buying roles differ, although both manufacture and sell physical goods.

Greif makes industrial bulk packaging and reconditions containers, while UFP's main business is medical devices and engineered components/protective packaging. Both manufacture and sell goods, but their core buyers and packaging orders do not materially overlap.

Greif makes industrial packaging and related container services, while Owens Corning's main business is roofing, insulation and glass-fiber composites. Both manufacture and sell goods, but their products and core buying customers differ.

Greif manufactures industrial packaging and related container services, while MSC's main business is distributing MRO tools and supplies. Both sell goods to industrial businesses, but packaging buyers are not purchasing the same order or generally acting in the same buying role as MSC's MRO buyers, and Greif manufactures while MSC distributes.

Greif manufactures industrial packaging and containers, while Flowserve’s main business is engineered flow-control equipment. Both manufacture and sell goods to industrial companies, but packaging buyers are not the same buying role as the plant engineering and maintenance buyers of pumps and valves.

Greif manufactures industrial packaging and containerboard, while Astec's main business is road-building and aggregate-processing machinery. Their buyers and purchase roles differ, despite both primarily manufacturing and selling physical goods.

Greif manufactures industrial packaging and related services, while Eastern makes engineered hardware, locks and castings. Their manufacturing revenue model and chain position align, but the products and buying roles do not.

Greif manufactures industrial packaging and container products, while ESAB's main business is welding and cutting equipment and consumables. Both sell manufactured goods, but their buyers purchase for different needs and in different roles.

Greif’s main business is industrial packaging containers, while CSW mainly makes HVAC/R, plumbing, electrical and building products. Their principal buying roles do not overlap, though both manufacture and sell goods.

Greif manufactures industrial packaging and containers, while Thermon’s main business is industrial heat-tracing and process-heating systems. Both manufacture goods for industrial companies, but their buyers and purchasing roles are different.

Compared Greif's manufactured industrial packaging with EACO/Bisco's distribution of electronic components, fasteners and hardware. They sell goods to manufacturers, but the buyers procure different inputs and EACO is a distributor rather than a packaging manufacturer.

Compared Airbnb's accommodation-booking marketplace with IAC's main digital publishing and media business. IAC's Angi marketplace serves homeowners seeking home services, not travelers or lodging hosts, and IAC mainly earns advertising and subscription revenue.

Airbnb operates a traveler-and-host accommodation marketplace, while Thryv primarily sells SaaS and marketing services to small local businesses. Their buyers, monetization, and role in the chain do not overlap.

Airbnb’s main marketplace arranges lodging bookings, while CarGurus’ main marketplace serves car shopping and dealer advertising/listings. Both operate as marketplaces, but they serve different orders and buyer roles, and CarGurus primarily earns dealer listing and advertising revenue rather than lodging-booking fees.

Airbnb’s lodging-and-experiences booking marketplace and Cars.com’s automotive marketplace serve different orders and distinct buyer roles. Both operate as marketplace intermediaries, but Cars.com mainly earns dealer subscriptions, advertising, and software/marketing-tool revenue rather than Airbnb’s booking fees.

Airbnb is a marketplace arranging accommodation bookings for travelers and hosts; Live Nation produces and operates live events and sells tickets. Concert attendees and event-industry clients are not the same buyers or buying need as Airbnb's lodging customers.

Airbnb operates a fee-based marketplace for lodging and experiences, while The ONE Group operates and licenses restaurants and bars. Restaurant dining is a different customer need and the companies occupy different commercial models and chain steps.

Compared Airbnb's lodging-booking marketplace with EverQuote's insurance-lead marketplace. Travelers and hosts are not buying insurance leads or policies for the same need; both are intermediaries, but Airbnb earns booking fees while EverQuote sells leads to insurers and agents.

Compared Airbnb's lodging-and-experiences marketplace with Intuit's financial software platform. Travelers and accommodation hosts are not buying tax, accounting, or payroll software in the same role, and the companies' primary revenue models and chain roles differ.

Airbnb operates a lodging marketplace charging booking fees, while Upbound provides lease-to-own household goods and financial access. Travelers seeking accommodations are not the same buyers or buying need as credit-challenged consumers leasing furniture and appliances.

Airbnb operates a lodging-and-experiences marketplace for travelers and hosts, while CSGS provides enterprise billing, payments and customer-engagement software and managed services. Their products, buyers, revenue mechanisms and positions in the chain do not overlap.

Compared Airbnb's lodging marketplace with NCR Voyix's commerce software, POS hardware and services business. Airbnb’s guests and accommodation hosts are not NCR Voyix’s merchant buyers, and the companies earn fees versus subscriptions, hardware sales and services.

Compared Airbnb's lodging-and-experiences marketplace with Emerald's B2B trade-show and event business. Travelers and accommodation hosts are not Emerald's exhibitor, sponsor, and professional-attendee buyers.

Compared Airbnb's accommodation-and-experience marketplace with MSGE's venue ownership and live-entertainment operations. Travelers and lodging hosts cannot place the same order with MSGE, whose main buyers attend or organize events rather than book accommodations.

Airbnb intermediates lodging bookings between hosts and travelers, while Taboola intermediates digital advertising placements between advertisers and publishers. Their buyers and products differ, though both operate transaction-based platforms that earn fees/revenue shares as intermediaries.

Airbnb’s main business is a lodging marketplace for travelers and hosts, while Cantaloupe provides cashless-payment hardware, software, and processing to unattended-retail operators. They serve different buyers and occupy different value chains.

CRA provides economic consulting and expert testimony for legal, regulatory, and strategy matters, while EPAM's main business is software and digital-platform engineering. Both sell professional services directly to enterprises, but their buyers are typically legal/regulatory or business leaders versus technology and digital teams.

CRA provides economic consulting and expert testimony for legal, regulatory and business matters, while Tetra Tech's main business is technical engineering and environmental project services. Both earn project-service fees and serve clients directly, but their buyers are typically in different roles.

Compared CRA's economic/legal and regulatory consulting with Grid Dynamics' digital transformation and software engineering services. Both earn consulting/service fees and deliver services directly, but their offerings and the buyer roles they serve differ.

Compared CRA's economic consulting and expert testimony for litigation and regulatory matters with Booz Allen's federal management, technology, engineering and mission consulting. Both sell professional services, but their main offerings and the client buying roles they serve differ.

CRA provides economic and litigation/regulatory consulting and expert testimony, while Legence's main business is engineering, installation and maintenance of building MEP systems. Their buyer roles differ—legal, corporate strategy and regulatory buyers versus facilities and building-system buyers—even where industries overlap.

CRA provides economic consulting and expert testimony for legal, regulatory, and strategic matters; Stagwell's main business is marketing, advertising, and communications services. Their corporate and public-sector buyers use them in different buying roles, despite both primarily earning service fees.

CRAI provides economic consulting and litigation/regulatory expert support, while Omnicom’s main business is advertising and marketing agency services. Both sell professional services directly to corporations, but the relevant legal, regulatory, and strategy buyers are not the same marketing and brand buyers.

CRA's main business is economic and litigation/regulatory consulting and expert testimony, while DFIN's is regulatory-reporting and compliance software and filing services. Their client categories overlap broadly, but the buying roles and the products purchased differ.

CRA provides economic consulting and expert testimony for litigation, regulatory, and transaction matters, while Franklin Covey’s main business is organizational leadership and training content. Their buyers are in different roles, and Franklin Covey primarily monetizes subscriptions and training offerings.

CRA provides economic consulting and expert testimony for legal, corporate and regulatory matters; TIC mainly tests, inspects and certifies physical infrastructure and assets. Their buyer roles differ, although both primarily earn fees for directly delivered professional services.

CRA International provides economic consulting and expert testimony, while Silvercrest’s main business is investment management and wealth planning. Their buyers and fee-generating service models are distinct.

CRA International provides economic, financial, and litigation/regulatory consulting and expert testimony, while Concentrix’s main business is outsourced customer-experience operations. Both earn service fees and directly serve enterprise clients, but their offerings and buying roles do not overlap.

CRA provides economic consulting and expert testimony for legal, regulatory, and strategic matters; Baldwin mainly distributes and brokers insurance. Corporate buyers use them in different roles, and Baldwin primarily earns insurance distribution commissions rather than consulting fees.

Compared CRA's economic consulting and litigation/regulatory expert services with Amentum's engineering, technical operations and program-management services. They both sell professional services, but Amentum's main government buyers procure operational and technical work rather than CRA's economic-advisory and expert-testimony work.

CRAI provides economic consulting and expert testimony, while CSGS’s main business is SaaS and managed billing, payments, and monetization systems. Their buyers and purchasing roles do not overlap meaningfully.

Deckers sells branded footwear and apparel, while Church & Dwight’s main business is branded household and personal-care consumables. Both sell goods as brand owners through retail channels, but they address different consumer needs and retail buying roles.

Compared Deckers’ branded footwear and apparel with BellRing’s branded protein shakes and powders. They sell different goods to consumers for different needs; both primarily sell branded goods made by contract manufacturers.

Deckers sells branded footwear and apparel, while Olaplex's main business is branded hair-care products, so a buyer cannot substitute the same order. Their consumer needs and specialist retail/salon buyers differ, though both sell branded goods made by contractors through retail and direct channels.

Compared Deckers’ branded footwear and apparel business with Cricut’s crafting machines, materials and software. Their consumer segments and products serve different needs, though both primarily sell branded goods made by contract manufacturers.

Deckers is a branded footwear/apparel company, while Dorman sells automotive replacement parts; buyers cannot substitute one for the other and their retail/distribution customers differ. Both primarily sell sourced branded goods and sit as product brand owners/manufacturers.

Deckers sells branded footwear and apparel, while Simply Good Foods sells branded nutrition snacks and shakes. Their consumer needs and category buyers differ, despite both being contract-manufactured branded goods sold through retail channels.

Deckers sells branded footwear and apparel, while Reynolds makes household foil, bags and disposable cookware. They both sell goods through retail channels, but the products and buying roles are different.

Deckers sells branded footwear, apparel and accessories, while B&G Foods' main business is branded packaged foods. Their retail and consumer buyers purchase for different needs, though both primarily sell branded goods they manufacture/contract-manufacture.

Deckers sells branded footwear and apparel through retail and wholesale channels, whereas Herbalife’s main business is direct-selling nutrition and personal-care products. Their consumer needs and buying roles differ; both sell goods, but Herbalife’s distributor-led channel is not Deckers’ brand-owner retail/wholesale step.

Deckers is a branded footwear and apparel maker/marketer, while Savers’ main business is retailing secondhand clothing and household goods. Both sell goods, but thrift shoppers are not the same buying segment and Savers is a retailer rather than the brand owner/manufacturer.

Deckers sells branded footwear and apparel, while Hormel's main business is branded packaged food. Their end-consumer needs and retail buying roles differ, though both principally manufacture/brand goods for sale.

Compared Deckers' branded footwear and apparel business with CSW's industrial HVAC/R, plumbing and specialty products. Their products and buying roles do not overlap, though both primarily sell manufactured goods and operate as product makers.

Deckers designs and sells branded footwear, apparel and accessories, while Tootsie Roll manufactures and sells confectionery. Both sell goods as brand manufacturers, but footwear buyers are not buying candy for the same need or through the same purchasing role.

Compared Deckers' branded footwear and apparel business with McCormick's spices, seasonings and flavor-products business. They both sell branded goods made under their brands, but neither the product order nor the relevant consumer or retail buyer is the same.

Deckers’ branded consumer footwear and apparel are not substitutes for Zebra’s enterprise inventory and workflow hardware. Both principally sell manufactured goods as brand owners, but to different buyers and for different needs.
Compared NVR's homebuilding and home sales with Stewart's title insurance and transaction-settlement services. The same homebuyers can use both, but they cannot buy a newly built home from Stewart.

NVR builds and sells homes directly to individual homebuyers, while CSW mainly manufactures building-system components for contractors, distributors and OEMs. Both principally earn revenue by selling manufactured goods and operate as makers, but neither the order nor the buyer overlaps.

NVR builds and sells homes directly to individual homebuyers, while Comfort Systems is a commercial mechanical contractor serving building owners and general contractors. Their offerings, buyers, revenue activity, and position in the construction chain differ.

Compared NVR’s homebuilding and direct sale of homes to individual buyers with Owens Corning’s manufacture of roofing, insulation, and composites. Owens Corning supplies builders and contractors rather than offering homes to NVR’s homebuyers, and is upstream in the construction chain.

NVR builds and sells finished homes to individual homebuyers, while Carlisle’s main business manufactures commercial roofing and building-envelope materials for contractors and distributors. Both primarily sell goods they make, but serve different buyers and orders.

Compared NVR's homebuilding business with Old Republic's insurance and title operations. Homebuyers can buy title insurance during the same transaction, but Old Republic does not sell homes and mainly earns insurance premiums and service fees.

NVR builds and sells homes to individual homebuyers, while IES's main business is electrical and mechanical contracting and equipment for developers, contractors and operators. IES does not offer homes to the same buyer role and primarily earns service/contracting revenue at a different chain step.

NVR builds and sells homes, while American Coastal underwrites residential property insurance. Homebuyers and insurance policyholders may overlap as households, but they buy for different needs and roles.

NVR builds and sells homes to individual homebuyers, while Deere's main business is manufacturing equipment for farmers, contractors and related users. Both primarily sell manufactured goods and sit as makers, but their products and buying needs do not overlap.

NVR builds and sells homes to individual homebuyers, while RMR primarily provides fee-based management services to REITs and real-estate companies. Their buyers, revenue models, and roles in the real-estate chain differ.
NVR builds and sells homes to homebuyers, while Goosehead distributes personal insurance policies. Home purchase buyers are not buying insurance in the same role or for the same need.

NVR builds and sells finished homes to individual homebuyers; Ferguson’s main business distributes building and plumbing/HVAC supplies to contractors and builders. Both principally sell goods, but they serve different buyers and occupy different chain steps.

NVR builds and sells residential homes to individual homebuyers, while Legence provides MEP engineering, installation, and maintenance services for institutional and commercial facility owners. Their products, buyers, revenue models, and positions in the construction chain differ.
NVR builds and sells new homes to homebuyers, while Angi operates a marketplace for homeowners to find repair, remodeling, and maintenance providers. The buyers, monetization, and chain roles differ.

NVR builds and sells new homes to individual homebuyers, while APi's main business is maintaining and installing building-systems services for commercial, industrial, and public-sector operators. Their products, buyers, revenue models, and chain roles differ.
